question: What is a data fabric architecture, how does it differ from a modern data warehouse, and when should an organisation move to one?
contributions: Serra's definition of data fabric against Gartner's
Eight technologies that move an MDW toward a fabric

results.claim: Serra places the threshold at three of the eight technologies for calling an MDW a data fabric, and admits there is no bright line.
results.setup: Serra's own definition and opinion, no measurement; eight features listed on p.152
results.quote: Personally, I call it a data fabric architecture if it uses at least three of those eight technologies.

results.claim: Data fabric is the most widely used architecture for new cloud solutions, especially for large data (over 10 terabytes).
results.setup: Serra's own definition and opinion, no measurement; no survey or source given
results.quote: Data fabric is the most widely used architecture for new solutions being built in the cloud, especially for large amounts of data (over 10 terabytes).

limits: Opinion chapter with no measurements; the 10 TB and three-of-eight thresholds are Serra's personal judgement.
No author, title, publisher or year printed in the excerpt; attribution rests on external knowledge plus cross-references (Chapters 6, 9, 10; Figure 10-2; 'my definition').
Figure 11-1 is an image; its content is not in the text.
Gartner definition quoted without citation or date.
practices: Call an architecture a data fabric if it uses at least three of the eight technologies (p.152).
Treat data virtualization as optional and use it for only a small number of situations (p.155).
Route all data requests through access policies via APIs, drivers or virtualization (p.154).
Use APIs instead of connection strings so moving data does not break callers (p.155).
Wrap reusable cleaning/ingestion code in services (p.156).
Before moving from MDW, evaluate needs, ROI, strategy and in-house expertise (p.157).
Focus on data fabric architectures as they exist today, not Gartner's intelligent fabric (p.151).

terms.definition: an evolution of the modern data warehouse (MDW) architecture: an advanced layer built onto the MDW to enhance data accessibility, security, discoverability, and availability
a set of guidelines, rules, and procedures that control who has access to what information, how that information may be used, and when access can be granted or denied
a repository that stores information about data assets, including their structure, relationships, and characteristics
a record of the history of any given piece of data, including where it came from, how it was transformed, and where it is stored
the process of collecting, consolidating, and maintaining consistent and accurate data from various sources within a company to create a single authoritative source for master data
a software architecture that allows applications and end users to access data from multiple sources as if it were stored in a single location
